prize_parts.citation: For introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and for showing how exporting decisions and reallocation across firms shape productivity and the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part B038 prize for Helpman and Melitz. The discussion did not change my ranking, but it did tighten the citation. The founding contribution is the selection-and-reallocation mechanism. Heterogeneous firms face fixed costs of exporting, so only the more productive firms export, and trade opening shifts market share toward them and raises aggregate productivity. This gives a welfare channel beyond the one in earlier new trade theory. It also produces sharp, testable predictions about who exports, who enters and exits, and who invests abroad (Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple). Those predictions have been tested for more than twenty years on customs and production microdata in many countries. I weight the robustness of the qualitative mechanism, not any particular estimate of the gains from trade, which depend on elasticity assumptions. On the chair's question about Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, I separate two things. The empirical facts on exporter premia and the Ricardian quantitative framework are important, but the heterogeneous-firm selection model is the identifiable discovery, and the citation should be worded around it. On the chair's question about a common standard, I apply the same test to B038 and B015. The question is whether the discovery is distinct from the earlier prizes, not whether the field has been recognised before. The 2008 prize covered scale economies and the location of production. B038 changes the unit of analysis, adds a different welfare channel and has been confirmed on micro data, so I read it as a successor. B015 also builds on earlier work on expectations, time consistency and policy rules. That is a point against it only if its building blocks are not distinct, and I find that harder to settle there. My own work on price adjustment is relevant to this view. The micro evidence on Calvo-type time-dependent pricing is mixed, so I cannot read the framework's endurance as confirmation of its specific building blocks. For B038, the micro evidence supports the core mechanism more directly.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the main reservation. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have serious claims on closely related work, and a two-name prize could be read as under-crediting them. I cannot fully resolve this. A narrow citation limits what is claimed but cannot make the omission disappear. Redding's quantitative and spatial extensions are real, but they extend the founding framework, so I would not add him. Second, welfare magnitudes are model-dependent, so the citation must not rest on them. Third, B015 has a larger footprint on policy practice than B038, and a committee that weights policy influence above attribution clarity could reasonably put B015 first. Fourth, Helpman's separate appearance on B030, which is not on the shortlist, means his credit has to be accounted for once. I do not think this weakens the B038 case, but it needs to be stated in the final citation process. Finally, my first choice in the opening ballot, B035, remains mature and broadly used. I cannot draw a clean three-name boundary for it, and no colleague ranked it, so I keep it only as an alternative.

responses.point: Fredriksson responded to my B036 proposal of Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He argues that the narrow China-shock framing puts Dorn in and Katz out, while the broader technology, tasks and trade framing puts Katz in and Dorn out. He prefers the broader framing and would not oppose Dorn instead of Katz.
responses.response: I accept the boundary point, and it is why B036 stays an alternative I do not prefer. My opening trio followed the trade-shock evidence, while your broader framing treats the skill-premium and task work as part of one discovery. I do not think the evidence settles which reading is correct. Whichever way the three names are chosen, a core contributor is left out, and the Acemoglu-Restrepo task lineage sits outside the credited set. I agree that the debates over shift-share inference have refined the estimates more than they have overturned the qualitative findings on local adjustment. The persistence of those effects is still contested, and that contest bears on maturity. B036 therefore has a harder attribution problem than B038, even though the evidence in it is high quality.

responses.point: Hassler keeps B015 first as a three-name prize for Woodford, Taylor and Calvo. He argues that the record is dated contributions tested over four decades. He treats the heterogeneous-agent critique as an extension, and he proposes that a citation be worded around foundations and not around current empirical performance of the simple model.
responses.response: I accept that wording the citation around foundations deals with part of the post-2021 problem. I still hold two reservations. First, the credited contributions are different kinds of work separated by decades. Calvo's pricing rule is a tractable device, and the micro evidence on time-dependent versus state-dependent adjustment, including my own work with you on menu costs, does not support reading it as an empirical finding. A citation praising the pricing foundation is hard to write without implying more empirical support than exists. Second, a framework that survives and adapts shows it is useful. It does not show that the three credited building blocks were the decisive steps. I am not saying B015 is weaker in scientific weight, and I would not object on merit if the committee settles the citation. I am saying the attribution question is more open there than for B038, so I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Enflo keeps B038 first and argues that the 2008 prize covered scale economies, product differentiation and the location of production, not firm-level selection. She says the citation should be built around the mechanism and not around the size of welfare gains. She leaves out Redding to keep the citation focused.
responses.response: I agree with the mechanism-based wording and with leaving out Redding, and my citation follows that logic. I would add one qualification to your point that the qualitative result is better supported than any single magnitude. The strongest empirical support is for selection and reallocation as channels. It is weaker for the claim that the welfare gains are large, which depends on parameters such as the trade elasticity. The citation should say what the model explains and avoid implying a measured size. Eight members ranking B038 is, as you say, a reason to test the case further, and I have not treated it as evidence of merit.

responses.point: Strömberg keeps B050 first as a two-name prize for Kiyotaki and Moore. He argues that attribution is clean, that the accelerator line is partly covered by the 2022 prize, and that direct empirical identification of the amplification mechanism is mixed. His opening ranked B038 eighth, and he asks whether the 2008 prize reduces the appetite for another trade prize.
responses.response: I agree that the two-name Kiyotaki-Moore attribution is cleaner than B015 and comparable to B038, and I would weigh that advantage. My difference is on evidence. You describe B050 as theory-led with mixed direct identification of the collateral channel. B038 differs in kind because its central mechanism generates predictions that were taken to micro data and held up on selection and reallocation. I would apply one standard to both. A theory-led mechanism can merit a prize, but the committee should say plainly what has and has not been tested. On the 2008 overlap, I think the real question is whether the later work is a different discovery. I read it as one, because it changes the unit of analysis and the welfare channel. Your question about the overlap with the 2022 prize is a similar judgement for B050, and I do not think it is settled against your candidate.

responses.point: Krusell calls B015 the strongest case on the shortlist. He argues that the framework's extension through financial frictions and heterogeneity without overturning its core shows durable scientific content, and he proposes framing Calvo and Taylor as the origin of nominal rigidity and the policy rule, with Woodford as the synthesis.
responses.response: Your origin-plus-synthesis framing is the cleanest defence of B015, and I accept it as the best available trio. My reservation is the one you name yourself. Extension without displacement shows adaptability, and it is weaker evidence for the specific credited steps. The three-name limit also leaves out the estimation work that made the framework usable. I give that cost more weight than you do because the credit gap is larger than in B038, where two names carry most of the identifiable theoretical contribution. I also note that you and Hassler are long-standing co-authors, so I do not treat your agreement as independent evidence.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as so central to firm-heterogeneity trade that a Helpman-Melitz prize would be seen as incomplete. A narrow citation reduces but does not remove this risk.

Whether the 2008 prize on new trade theory reduces the case for another trade award. I read B038 as a distinct successor, but this is a judgement the committee should make explicitly and under the same standard it applies to B015.
How much of the qualitative selection and reallocation result, and how little of the welfare magnitude, should be cited as established.
Whether B015 should rank above B038 if the committee settles on one trio and one citation wording. I would not oppose it on scientific grounds.
How far my industrial-organisation and international-pricing background biases my weighting of firm-level trade, of B035 and of the pricing side of B015.
I rely on general knowledge and the supplied round-1 statements. I have not independently verified any claim about the scientific record or credit.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure from the supplied profile: I co-authored a 2026 IJIO paper on menu costs and asymmetric price adjustment with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen. Hassler prefers B015, which I treat as an alternative and not my preferred part, and I weigh his arguments as evidence only. I am married to Magdalena Andersson, a public fact for which the profile gives no evidence of any bearing on committee work. I share an SSE affiliation with Dreber Almenberg, Strömberg and Andersson (Tommy). My research field of international pricing, trade and industrial organisation is close to B038, B035 and the pricing side of B015, and I flag this as a possible bias. I find no co-authorship or institutional tie to Helpman, Melitz or Redding, or to the credited names on B015 and B035. No recusal-requiring connection is apparent from the supplied profile, and I disclose these ties without adjudicating them.
